title: Pregnancy scanning ewes
subtitle: Knowing whether a ewe carries one, two, or three lambs changes what you feed her in the final six weeks. That knowledge pays for the scanner's visit many times over.
excerpt: Pregnancy scanning uses ultrasound to count the lambs in each ewe between day 60 and day 90 of gestation. A scanner with a trained operator reads a transabdominal scan in seconds: dry (not pregnant), single, twin, or triplet. The result goes into the flock register and drives the late-pregnancy feeding plan. Here is how the session runs and how to use the results.
sourceNotes: AHDB Beef and Lamb, Better Returns Programme, Pregnancy Scanning guide. SAC Consulting, ewe nutrition in late pregnancy notes. DEFRA Codes of Recommendations for the Welfare of Sheep. NADIS advisory on ewe nutrition and scanning.

glossaryTerms.definition: Transabdominal ultrasound pregnancy diagnosis in sheep, carried out between day 60 and 90 of gestation. A trained scanner applies gel and a probe to the ewe's underside in front of the udder and counts the foetuses on screen.
A ewe carrying two lambs. Twin-bearing ewes need significantly higher late-pregnancy nutrition than singles to prevent twin-lamb disease (pregnancy toxaemia).

Metabolic disease in late-pregnancy ewes, also called twin-lamb disease. Caused by insufficient energy in the diet when the lambs' glucose demands peak in the last 4–6 weeks. Most common in underfed multiple-bearing ewes.

content.text: Pregnancy
scanning
turns late-pregnancy feeding from guesswork into a calculation. A ewe with triplets needs three times the supplement of a dry ewe. Without scanning, you either underfeed triplet ewes and risk
pregnancy toxaemia
, or overfeed dry ewes and get difficult lambings.
When to scan

The optimal window is day 60-90 of gestation. Before day 60 the foetuses are too small to count reliably; after day 90 they begin to overlap in the scan image and triplets may be read as twins. If you put the ram in on 1 November, scan from 31 December to 29 January.
Preparing for the scanning session
Withhold feed for 12-18 hours before scanning. A rumen full of recently eaten feed makes the scan image harder to read and increases 'dry' misclassifications.
Gather all ewes into a handling race or crowding pen. The scanner works fastest when animals move through steadily without doubling back.
Have a marking system ready before the scanner arrives, spray paint in three colours for dry / single / twins-and-above is a common convention. Agree it with the scanner beforehand.
Record each ewe's ear tag and scan result as she comes through. A small flock can be recorded on a clipboard; a larger flock benefits from a per-ear-tag entry in the flock register.
Using the scan results
Separate ewes into feeding groups: dry, single, and
twin-bearing
(including triplets). Feed groups separately for the last 6 weeks of gestation. A standard late-pregnancy supplementary concentrate allowance:
Dry ewes: no concentrate supplement needed on good quality hay.
Single-bearing: 200-300 g concentrate per day from 6 weeks before lambing, rising to 400 g in the final 2 weeks.
Twins: 400-600 g per day from 6 weeks, rising to 600-800 g in the final 2 weeks.
Triplets: 600-800 g per day from 6 weeks, rising to 800 g-1 kg in the final 2 weeks.
These figures assume reasonable-quality hay is available ad lib. Adjust down if ewes gain weight, up if they lose condition. Check body condition score fortnightly in the last 6 weeks.
